utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technicians. Good morning to the interpreters. We shall now resume our work. Mr. Dubuisson, please, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances please, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours, please, my name is Mr. Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Meddegoda and Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Mr. Goran Mikulicic and I appear for the Defence together with my colleague Mr. Joka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence calls witness Tomislav Rajic to the stand. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (No translation).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rajic, can you hear me now? Thank you very much for coming and I do apologise for their technical problems. They often come up. You have to understand that there are some interpreters here, but we don't share the same language. You will now read out the solemn declaration that the usher is holding out for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tomislav Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For the moment being, Mr. Rajic, I will ask you to answer the questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic for the Defence. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rajic. As Your Honours have already told you, I am going to ask you several questions as the Defence counsel and I would like to ask you to answer them to the best of your ability. Mr. Rajic, could you please tell us where and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of May, 1959 in Vucija Gora of the Municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What are you by nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By nationality I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you religious, Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, I am a believer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which denomination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you went to primary school and what further education you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to primary school in Travnik, where I also went to secondary school and I graduated from the faculty of law in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you graduated from the school of law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you do military service in the former Yugoslav Peoples Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when and where you did your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did my military service in Bileca, in the school for reserve officers from the 8th of August, 1984 to the 5th of July, 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you left the school for reserve officers, did you receive a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a reserve lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you went to work after you graduated from the faculty of law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I waited for a job for one year and then I, for one year, I worked in a firm dealing with agriculture production and then I went to the army, joined the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, after graduation, you worked as a legal officer in a firm and then you did military service for one year. When you returned from the army, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I once again went back to the same firm where I remained until the 4th of October, 1990, after which, I went to the municipality and became an assistant to the secretary for national defence of the municipal secretariat for Travnik -- for the defence secretariat in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am going to ask you, Mr. Rajic, to speak a little more slowly and make a break between the sentences, so that our interpreters can follow you better. Thank you. So you told us that from 1990 you found employment in the municipal structures and that you were employed in duties in the secretariat for national defence. Can you tell us, please, Mr. Rajic, what kind of duties the secretariat for defence had? What was its basic function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me say at the outset that I came as an assistant, but on the 22nd of February, 1991, that is to say after the first elections, I was nominated for secretary. That is the number one man of the secretariat. The basic function of the municipal secretariat for national defence was to make records of all reservists and civil defence reservists, the duties for the conscripts, material obligations and serving in the centres of the OIO, which was, at the time reconnaissance, the reconnaissance service and the intelligence service. That means that these municipal secretariats were, in fact, a service for the other services and units of the Yugoslav Peoples Army, the units of Territorial Defence, the units for civil defence, which were general and specialised for the conscripts because, according to the regulations at that time, it was envisaged that certain services, certain firms, should continue their work in case of war and faced with the threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, thank you. So the basic function, in fact, of the body in which you were employed and whose chief you became was, in fact, to perform certain duties which were prescribed by law. By which law were these duties prescribed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were several laws governing our duties and responsibilities. The basic law, the basic two laws, according to which all of us in the former Yugoslavia was the law on all peoples defence and social service protection. And the second law was conscription, the law on conscription regarding recruitment and record, the keeping of records on the reserve formations. And let me also say that there was some other regulations which were of lesser importance than these two laws, which further regulated in greater detail the various regions and areas to which these two laws pertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll say more about that later on, Mr. Rajic, thank you. Would you now please tell us in conformity with the law on conscripts, what was this law and who were the conscripts? To whom did it refer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was not only the law governing conscripts, there were five responsibilities: one was the military responsibility, the professional responsibility, the responsibility to serve in the units of civil defence units or for materiel donations and in the OIO services that I mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, could you please repeat the second duty, because I am not sure that it was introduced into the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the working duties, the service duties. And that is the first duty after the conscript duty. And this service duty envisaged work in definite companies, public organisations and institutions which would come into function in case of war and when the threat of war was imminent, but it was also a service responsibility for the formation of certain platoons and taking part in the assessing of the terrain and fortifications for the terrain. In mopping up operations and all for the armed forces at a given point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Later on we'll come back to that, Mr. Rajic, and we'll speak about it in greater detail. I would just like to present a general picture of the situation. So you said that you began performing these functions in 1990 and are you still performing those duties or do you have some other duties to perform today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked until the 1st of January, 1994, as the head of department for defence and at the present point in time I am performing the duties of the president of the municipal assembly in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In view of your formal training and education, you have graduated from the faculty of law and in view of your work experience, we can say that you are well acquainted with the laws that we're discussing and the regulations that we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know the laws and regulations very well, but let me say that more than four years have elapsed since that time, so I am not well acquainted with the details, but I do have a general overview of the laws and regulations that exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Trial Chamber will hear that later on. Mr. Rajic, let us now go back to the events of the end of 1992 and the first half of 1993 in the region. I have in mind the events, the relationship between the Croatian and Muslim population in particular. At that time, the war had already started in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the one hand we had the attackers in the form of the Yugoslav Peoples Army and the Serbian formations. On the other hand we had the defence set up in which the citizens of the Croatian and Muslim citizens took part. Can you give us briefly an overview of the events at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the war in the region where I was located began by a Serbian attack on Travnik. And Travnik was the centre of the Lasva River Valley on the 19th of April, 1992, with an attack on a settlement, Turbe. With the beginning of the war in Slovenia and later on in Croatia, it was quite evident because the units of the JNA withdrew from those regions and they came to the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the barracks that were in that region as they were in Travnik, in Busovaca and the other barrack locations. And we, the Croatian people, who were there in that location, we knew and we felt that if the war was going to be as it had been in Croatia and if the Serbs had pretensions towards Croatia, then in no event would they leave Bosnia-Herzegovina alone. And we, therefore, tried to prepare ourselves. And the first thing that we did was to erect the facilities for the reserve police, the units for the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, Mr. Rajic. You said that the Croatian people started to prepare because they felt that there would be a conflict, which in Croatia was already underway. Could you tell us about the situation with the Muslim population? Did they also undergo preparations? Did you have contacts with the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The period I am talking about, I mean preparations through joint institutions. That is to say, there were members of the Muslim people as well because they too felt that war was imminent and, therefore, they tried to organise, we tried to organise ourselves to meet that event. And then, when the first attack took place on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was sometime in September 1991 and it was an attack on the village of Ravno, the representatives, the leadership of the Muslim people, who were in the peaks of power, said that this was not their war. But with the beginning of 1992, in Travnik, and I say right up to 1992, we worked together in one way or another. We had the same organs, institutions, we tried to pool our efforts. And if the secretary for national defence was a Croat, for example, the commander of the Territorial Defence, was a Muslim. So we tried to divide up the duties and we were conditioned. However, in the spring of 1992, when the first, but fairly numerous people, groups, Muslims from the Bosnian/Krajina area began to arrive, the refugees, there was a sort of demographic unbalance, the demographic balance was upset, which had existed until that time. And the humanitarian assistance began to arrive, individuals carrying humanitarian assistance. But then we saw they were members of the Mujahedin, in fact. And they brought with them some new ideas to the region where these were not prevalent. And so this upset our cooperation and it was severed later on. Quite simply they felt that they could do without us. And, as I say, this upset our cooperation and the events that followed took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now we're talking about mid-1992, aren't we? Do you recall, Mr. Rajic, whether at that particular time, the ruling powers, the political powers of Bosnia-Herzegovina declared a state of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A state of war was proclaimed at the beginning of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, from March 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at the beginning of April, 1992 with the attack on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So we can say from April 1992 onwards, de facto, on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina a state of war was proclaimed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Rajic, that a considerable number of Muslims of the Muslim population came to the area of the Lasva River Valley because it was compelled to flee in the face of the Yugoslav Peoples Army and the Serbian military units. They fled to the area, could you tell us how many people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, many people passed through Travnik. Over 120.000 refugees and some of them, many of them remained in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And so, in this region there was a disbalance in the population ratio compared to the pre-war situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and this disbalance was drastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, Mr. Rajic, were the people who came to these areas where they never lived before, where did they live? Where did they go to? Where were they put up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the first wave, they were sent to collective centres. That is to say, schools, kindergartens, two kindergartens in town, sports halls and most of them, not many, but most of them were sent to the different villages, surrounding villages, and they stayed with the people of the area, the villages. So that the number, the population doubled in the villages around Travnik and Novi Travnik and in the Lasva River Valley itself as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, Mr. Rajic, according to the best of your recollections, what the relationship was between the Muslim and Croatian population in the area before the war and what the relationship was at the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, before the beginning of the war, according to the 1991 Muslim census, there was a slight advantage on the Muslim side. There were more Muslims than Croats, but a very slight majority. Including the Serbs, they just had a relative majority and it was 4 to 5 per cent more. According to the '91 population census. However, with the arrival these refugees and -- but as you know a population census is one thing. The Croats from this area are well-known as people who work in the countries of Western Europe. So that if we look at the military capable populace in certain municipalities, the ratio was 1 to 5 to the advantage of the Muslims, Bosnia Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. You mentioned that at the beginning on the side of the Muslim population, there was the prevalent idea that the conflicts with the JNA were not conflicts in which they ought to take part; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, in the leadership that was correct. However the people felt a little differently. Very early on they began to organise through the patriotic front which was set up, but unfortunately, it was based on religion more. It took a religious basis for its establishment and so very early on, parallelly, while we worked in the joint institutions, they had their patriotic front, which was religiously based, formed for themselves and for their purposes, and would form detachments later on which would become military detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in that way they, in fact, set up parallel organs of power and authority in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, whether they were parallel organs of authority, I don't know, but they were parallel, military formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Rajic, when these conflicts came out in the open between the Croats and the Muslims in that area, when they obviously came to disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everyone who had any sense in his mind had to fear an open conflict and war. There were certain incidents, and most of us thought that it would end with incidents, because that war, that conflict suited the Croats and the Muslim Bosniaks least of all. And this open conflict was proceeded by quite a few incidents of this nature. For example, in Travnik, in 1992, in October, although we were in separate units, we went together to help Jajce in Travnik, the commander of the municipal staff of Travnik, Colonel Ivica Stojak was killed. And then I think on the 17th of March, two members of the HVO were killed, Ivo Juric and Dragan Dzandara, if I'm not mistaken. And then in Travnik on the eve of Easter, 8th or 9th of April 1993, all Croat flags were burned, all of those that were flying on the occasion of the holiday. And a woman was killed in her apartment on that day, I think it was the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, there were quite a few incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, incidents. I'm talking about the ones that I'm very familiar with. But there were quite a few such incidents in these municipalities. So, there was also a road of salvation, as we called it, that went through the mountains; and before the fighting, five Croats simply disappeared there. They were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Rajic, to the best of your recollection, when did an all out attack by the Muslim military forces occur in the Busovaca area against the Croat units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection this was in January 1993, around the 20th, perhaps a bit after the 20th. I don't know exactly, but I know it was January. In Busovaca, even before that -- or rather in Travnik, before that, in '92, there was a conflict, and later it was in Busovaca that these hostilities broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in your opinion, why did the Muslim military forces attack the area of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard to say why. Probably, so as to capture this area. Simply to put under their control everything that might hamper someone's intentions at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Also there are some communication lines going through that area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the most important communication line going through this area, that is the communication line Jajce-Travnik-Zenica, and it also goes towards Sarajevo. And at any rate, from a military and strategic point of view, this is an exceptionally important area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Am I mistaken, Mr. Rajic, if I say that this communication line actually links together the territories that are predominantly populated with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it does, yes. On the eastern side, so to speak; Tusla, Kakanj, Zenica, that area. And this is populated by a Muslim majority population, but this communication line also proceeds towards Bugojno and Vakuf where in Donje Vakuf, for example, the Muslims were an absolute majority and in Bugojno they were a relative majority. At any rate, for Bosnia-Herzegovina this communication line was crucial in terms of east-west communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. So, at that time, during these events, you said that you worked as the head of the security for a national defence, and later it came to be known as the Department of Defence. What was your main function, your main task as you held this job during the war? And may I remind you that in April, 1992, a state of war was declared on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main function of all secretariats or departments of defence was to organise units, military units, and people who were supposed to be involved in work duty so that all of this could function, all together. So, it was our job to seek military conscripts and to give them their exact war assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, correct me if I'm wrong, but as this function was to be carried out, there were certain lists, certain records that were kept for the secretariats in the various municipalities; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true. All military abled men, those who were capable of serving in the armed forces and those who weren't, had their files with their basic data, name, surname, date of birth, place of birth, whether he was capable or incapable of military service, their address, their current address, their permanent address; so, at every point in time we had to know where each and every man was at a given time, theoretically. But of course there were always some people whose whereabouts were unfamiliar to us, but these records were very important. You cannot claim that they were one hundred per cent accurate, but at any rate, they were very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Rajic, according to the law in force at that time, during what period in one's life would one have this kind of military duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the age of 17 a man would be registered in military records. When he would turn 18, then he would undergo a thorough medical examination to see whether he was capable of military service, and then he would be assigned the service where he would serve, whether it would be the navy or the army, et cetera. Then they would be sent to do their military service. And as a rule each and every one of these men would be assigned to a reserve unit, either the Territorial Defence or the JNA, it was all the same, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, until what age did this military service duty go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sixty, until the age of 60. When a man would turn 60, then his files would be sent to archives. As far as work duty is concerned, that would be assumed at the age of 16. And men up to the age of 65 were -- they had to take work duty. And on for women this obligation went up to the age of 55, but for men until the age of 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you're speaking about work duty and persons who were registered as people who had to carry out work duty, this is part of one's military obligations; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is part of the war assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you explain how this is part of war assignments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of this was aimed at the better functioning of the military forces. So, this was supposed to help the military units all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, in your introduction you mentioned to us that at that time, on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were certain regulations that were in force in this particular area. Tell me, were these regulations in force after the elections that were held and after the independence of Bosnia was proclaimed? Was this a new set of regulations, or was this a set of regulations that was in force in the former Yugoslavia and did the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina simply take them over like other republics did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were regulations in force in the territory of the entire former Yugoslavia, and after that republican regulations were passed that regulated this area, but perhaps in greater detail. And after the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was not only these regulations, but all other regulations governing other areas of life that were also taken over from the former Yugoslavia, because the parliament did not really have an opportunity to pass new laws. So all of this was taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. So, you said that the main laws in this area was the law on total national defence and social self protection and the law on conscription; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, you also mentioned that on the basis of these basic laws, the so-called bylaws were passed regulating this particular area in greater detail; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Rajic, I see that you have brought with you some papers. So, we currently ask the Court to allow the witness to use these papers during his testimony so that it could be as accurate as possible. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Of course it is possible. I think there is no objection from the Prosecution; is there, Mr. Neimann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I assume these are the papers that Mr. Mikulicic has shown us before. If they are, there is no problem. But if they are new papers, we haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mikulicic, can you confirm that these documents are those that you showed to the Prosecution before the hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour. These are not documents that the Defence wishes to tender as evidence for this court. These are simply notes to remind the witness of what he wishes to say during his testimony. So, these are not documents that the Defence wishes to tender as evidence. This is simply to remind the witness of what he wishes to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Then I think you can use them, Mr. Mikulicic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Rajic, we were talking about some of these bylaws that were passed on the basis of the laws that were in force at that particular point in time and that were taken over from the legislation of the former Yugoslavia. Could you tell me what these documents are, what these laws are, and what was regulated on the basis of these regulations, and in what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic law in this area was the law on total national defence, which was published in the official Gazette of the FSRY. So this is a federal law published in the official Gazette, number 21/82. On the basis of that law, republican law was passed, the law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on total national defence, which was published in the official Gazette, number 3/84. Amendments to this republican law were published in the official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina on number 17/87. However, on the basis of this federal law a decree was passed on organising work duty and implementing it, related to tasks within the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak slower for the sake of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, this was published in the official Gazette of the FSRY, number 35/83. And this decree regulates in detail the question of work duty, what it includes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Rajic, if I have understood you correctly, on the basis of these laws, a bylaw was also passed which explains in detail how work duty is carried out and what its purpose is. Could you tell us why it was necessary at all to establish units involving work duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, simply for the following reason: To carry out those duties that soldiers with guns in their hands cannot do. These are units that helped, I mean people who had work duty helped these military units with the aim of successfully organising defence or attack, depending on what was in question at that particular point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, these work duty units carried out some kind of work, which is quite obvious. And what does this bylaw say? What kind of work was to be carried out by these units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The best thing would be for me to quote this particular text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but speak slowly for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 6 of this federal decree says -- .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Neimann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It seems we have moved from what I understood to be notes, which I didn't seek to inspect at the time, into now referring to actual text. And I think, Your Honours, I would like to at least examine the documents that the witness is referring to before he does that. I assume they are in his own language, but I would like to see them before he quotes from them, unless Mr. Mikulicic seeks to lay the foundation of it. It's a bit of a disadvantage here when the witness is referring to material that is in front of him which purports to be presumably some sort of a law and none of us have access to that or know what its contents are. So my objection is based on this ground: Either Mr. Mikulicic lays a better foundation for the reference to the material, or alternatively we're given an opportunity to inspect it, Your Honours. That's my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think that maybe Mr. Mikulicic could make a copy of some of these documents and these could help you, Mr. Neimann, to follow the sayings of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would be grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, what do you think of my proposal? Is it possible for you to make a copy of the text that you are referring to so it will help the Prosecution follow our work? Actually maybe this would be a good time to take a break. And maybe, Mr. Mikulicic, during this break you could make a copy of these documents. The registry will of course help you in every way. Maybe this is the best way to proceed. We shall take a 20-minute break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, have you managed to solve your problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I am very grateful for Your Honours assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I continue my examination of the witness, let me give a brief explanation regarding the documents. We are discussing a document which the witness has brought with him with the intention of recalling regulations and norms from that time. I saw these documents yesterday and so I did not have enough time to prepare it and to comply with procedure, Court procedure. However, if the Trial Chamber agrees and if my learned colleague the Prosecutor agrees, the document that we have before us I would tender as evidence and I should like to ask the secretariat to translate the document, if possible. I think that would be the best way of having the document tendered into evidence in view of the fact that we are discussing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we have no difficulty with that. The only position I would ask for is that it not be formerly tendered until we've seen the translation of it. I don't expect there to be any objection to it. I have had it explained to me what it roughly is about. As a matter of formality, I wouldn't be likely to be consenting to the tender of a document I don't know the contents of. Subject to that, I think the course proposed by Mr. Mikulicic is very appropriate in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber agrees to this proposal. Mr. Mikulicic, you may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Rajic, having dealt with formalities, we are discussing a decree on the organisation and execution of work duties in connection with the tasks and duties for the needs of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You said that this decree was published in the official gazette of Yugoslavia and that the number was 35/83. And this you called the Federal Regulation of the Former Yugoslavia. Is it true, Mr. Rajic, that this former federal regulation, with the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was taken over as a republican regulation, a republican decree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, Mr. Rajic, you mentioned Article 4 of the decree. Could you tell us the purpose of the formation of units with work duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Articles 4, 6 and 7 speak of these work duties. And so I should like to quote Article 4, please. "Units and their work duties for the needs of the armed forces in war are organised in peace by a decree of the competent municipal organ, issued on the basis of a request by the competent military territorial organ. In wartime, if this is demanded by needs for the combat activities and other requirements of the armed forces and the competent municipal organ is not able to issue orders in the sense of Point 1 of this article, the units of the work duties are organised according to an order of the chief of the competent military territorial organ or by order of the military commander holding the position of commander or of that rank or of a higher rank. In the further text he is referred to as commander." And that is the end of the quotation of Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, could you explain to us as somebody working with these kind of affairs and somebody who applied this decree, what that means in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In practical terms it means something that I have already said. And that is that in peacetime, the municipal institutions for defence on the basis of a request by the military organs fills up and calls up for their purposes certain recruits when the need arises. However, in wartime, when all these links have been severed, these lines of communication have been severed or interrupted, because this was envisaged for a war with a foreign enemy, fighting a foreign enemy. Where we severed all the polls that existed in a municipality, then we were no longer able to act in this particular manner as was regulated in Article 1 of this decree, but we had to make shift and adjust ourselves to the existing situation. And, therefore, the commanders of the military units who needed recruits for work duties, specific work duties, they would seek ways and means of coming by these recruits and the simplest way was to use the military police, which would round up or collect these people and bring them in for war duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Mr. Rajic, what kind of duties and tasks did the units of the work duty, formations were they engaged in? What did these units do and to what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me quote part of Article 6, that will explain it best, perhaps. And that is that the work units, in performing their tasks and duties for the needs and purposes of the armed forces, can be engaged in the execution of the following tasks: "Number one, for performing work to fortifications and dealing with roads, railway lines, airports, other helodroms, ports, other ports, harbours, hydrodroms and so on. To build objects for war facilities for water and for water stations and water works. To camouflage water facilities and water supply systems. To camouflage facilities and ongoing civil engineering work. And to supply points of crossing waters and other waterways. To build up and maintain secret storehouses, bases, dugouts, hospitals and other sanitary first aid institution. And other engineering work in the regions and zones of where the combat activities exist in order to ensure the more successful performance of the war work duties of the armed forces." And let me also quote Point 7 of the same article. That is; "to execute other work duties for the needs of armed forces." End of quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in this article, taxitively (sic) speaking, it enumerates all the tasks and duties which the working duties imply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but in Point 7, it is stated that if other needs arise, depending on the commander of the particular unit, the commander can use his men for some other duties which have not been enumerated in that particular article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us recall that we're talking about the period when a state of war was proclaimed on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Article 6 states, among others, that; "the work duty units performed duties along the directions and in the regions of combat activity, which ensure the successful execution of the war tasks of the units of the armed forces." Does this formulation allow for the possibility of the work duty units being used for fortification work to dig trenches, dugouts and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is what emanates from the definition that you just gave us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does it also follow from the text of the law, the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (No translation).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage, I am going to object to this witness being called upon to give an interpretation of the law as such. What I will not object to is him being asked questions of how this law was interpreted at the particular time as a matter of fact. So if the witness is asked whether this law was interpreted to commit trench digging, for example, at that particular point in time and place, I won't object to that. But if this witness is being called upon generally to interpret the law and say as a matter of law, it is to be interpreted this way, then I object to that and I object to it on two grounds: One is that it is a conclusion that may ultimately fall to Your Honours to determine. And, secondly, I don't believe this witness has been adequately qualified for that purpose. That's my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I fully accept the attitude of my distinguished colleague, Mr. Niemann. And it is not the defence's intention to ask the witness to give a general explanation of a legal matter. But it is our intention to ask the witness as somebody who applied those regulations to see how these were applied in practice. Because it was the witness who by virtue of his professional function applied those rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So I think we all agree with what you've just said, Mr. Mikulicic, therefore, you may proceed. There is no problem, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shall in future try to avoid questions which would be an of a generally formulated nature and I will pose them in connection with the functions performed by the witness. I think that will satisfy my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So then, Mr. Rajic, let me ask you the following question: Did you, in the war events of 1993, on the basis of this decree, which we have quoted, did you call up recruits for their work duties? That is to say, to use them for digging trenches, dugouts and fortifications in the war zones for the needs of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Rajic, that when circumstances allowed, this invitation was done by courier, by telephone or in some other way, you would call up the recruits in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If the war situation and circumstances did not allow for this, then you sent military police to collect these individuals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, I should like to ask you to try to tell me from your practice whether individual commanders of parts of the battlefield, parts of the line, frontline, did they also call up individuals for digging trenches and fortification, did they also call up these work duty recruits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In which way? Do you know how they did this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we were dealing with -- for example, defence was organised in our region according to different sectors, so there was a certain area which was covered by a commander for several units, the commander of several units. And the commander would have to, as a rule, go to the commander of the brigade and he would ask for a certain number of individuals that he needed to perform certain work duties. And then, the commander of the brigade, via the military police, would go out and get these conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, from your experience, although the term "work duty" implies the conclusion that it is not a voluntary duty, voluntary work, was there prescribed by law any sanctions for individuals who would not comply with this invitation, with this request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was a violation of that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Refusal was a violation of the duty. Were there any sanctions for that violation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in peacetime, this would be qualified as a violation and there would be something, you would have to pay a fine, they would have to pay a fine or go to prison for a short time. But, in wartime, fines were, of course, completely obliterated, and so, for any violation of work duty regulations and requests, we had other types of sanctions. First of all, we would talk to the individual. We would explain to him that that was his work duty. If he continued to refuse, then he would be detained. And this was determined by the various commanders in the units, the length of detention and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long this detention could last for failure to comply with the work duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depending on the rank of the commander, commanders could issue penalties of 3 days' detention period. That with was the lowest for company commanders. And brigade commanders could issue 10 to 15 days' detention periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Rajic. So you're talking about the situation when a state of war was proclaimed, right? Tell me, although you spoke of that during your introductory remarks, but perhaps you could explain it to us in greater detail now. According to what criterion were certain people involved in the armed forces serving with a rifle in their hand, to speak figuratively, and according to which criterion did other people who did not carry a rifle in their hand have work duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the war in our country, which is of a special nature, I think, it was necessary to be fit from the point of view from health to serve in the armed forces with a rifle in the hand. So there were some people who were not fit for full military duty, but they were nevertheless involved. In the work duty units, there were elderly people, primarily. Those who were not fit for fighting. However, in these units, in the work duty units, there were people who belonged to different ethnic groups and who happened to be in a certain region and who did not wish to participate in armed conflicts with the members of their own ethnic group. And they certainly would not, therefore, be taken by the commanders of military units into these units. Because, in that case, there would be a possibility of subversive activity within the unit itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Rajic, tell us, when certain work duty units were composed, did one take into account the possible ethnic composition of such units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that particular attention was paid to ethnic composition of these units. People simply had to look at what was available at that point in time for such work duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Are you familiar with the Kaonik facility near Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the purpose of this facility was before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before it was a facility of the Yugoslav Peoples Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened after the JNA left the area and left this particular facility? What happened to the facility itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In it, the district prison was organised, I believe. That is what it was called. It was really a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Rajic, that in that district military prison, within this facility, in the first half of 1993, Muslim civilians from the area of Busovaca were interned, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it from hearsay, but I really don't know for sure. I was in Travnik, after all. I heard that Muslims were detained there too. But I know that we would primarily take disciplinary action against disobedient people of our own as I already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come to visit this facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came only in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then, I imagine that in 1993, you did not have the opportunity of meeting the warden of this facility or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you're not, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just tell us one more thing, Mr. Rajic, in view of the nature of the office you held, I believe that you were familiar with the armed units in that area and that you had contact with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In these contacts, did you ever see some soldiers who had insignia of the Croat army, HV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rajic, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann. Do you wish to put any questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rajic. Mr. Rajic, I wanted to see if you could assist me in clarifying the structure of things in terms of the defence of the former Yugoslavia that under the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia first. You were asked some questions about that by my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic. Now, I take it, it is correct, is it not, that there was the federal department of defence, if I could call it that, which was the federal department in the socialist federal republic; is that right? And then there came down to be a component of the defence department, which was in the individual republics themselves, in this case, it was the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And then it descended right then down to a municipal level and there was a component of defence in the municipal level and that was the position that you're in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what was the line, if any, of reporting in this process? Did you report to the department of defence in Sarajevo, being that of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Or did you report directly to the socialist federal republic in, presumably, located in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reports were directly given to the military district, as it was called then, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. And the military district, that was a federal district, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at the level of the republic, but it was a federal organ because it is the federal organs that are concerned as far as the army is involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course. And the army at that stage, now I am talking, really, say up to 1990. The army at that stage was the JNA? And the Territorial Defence is something that was much more local to yourself. Did you have any role or connection on a municipal level to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time I was secretary for national defence, and my secretariat was supposed to serve the Territorial Defence units as well as the JNA units, the civilian defence units, all of it in keeping with the military obligations I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I take it that when it came to mobilisation of the Territorial Defence, except in areas where you were calling on them for assistance in civil defence matters, that was not a matter that could be decided at the municipal level; am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. When it came to the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence, was that something you could do at the municipal level or did that decision have to be taken at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision really depended on different things. Actually, there were two kinds of Territorial Defence units; one were the municipal units which could be called up at the request of the executive council of the municipality after mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the work that -- that mobilisation, could that be directed to military matters, or could it only be directed to civil defence matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when it came to mobilisation of the Territorial Defence at the municipal level, was the executive of the municipality authorised to direct war operations? In other words, could it tell the Territorial Defence where it should fight and where it shouldn't, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me say that the executive branch, after the Serbs withdrew from government, was no longer the executive council that it was before that. And the executive council did not have that kind of authority any longer, because it didn't really exist. Only the name remained, executive council, but the rest didn't really function any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to move into that area of what happened after the breakup of the federation, but I just wanted to concentrate on the pre-breakup period, if I could, for the moment. Because you've been kind enough to bring the laws forward and I understand that you are familiar with them. Now, when it comes to the JNA, I take it you, this is again pre-1990, the executive committee of the municipality didn't have the authority to direct the JNA in its operations; did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Although, the JNA could come to the municipal authorities and seek assistance, or probably demand assistance, this is pre-1990, should that situation arise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, both the Territorial Defence and the JNA, prior to 1990, was a multi-ethnic, both were multi-ethnic organisations, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And indeed, they would deliberate, there was a deliberate policy of ensuring that there was a relatively even balance of ethnic groups in both those organisations, the Territorial Defence and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was taken into account, but whether this kind of balance was ensured; in the Territorial Defence unit, yes, but not in the JNA, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think history has shown in the JNA it was perhaps even abused, the principle, that is. Now, when Bosnia-Herzegovina became an independent country, all of this changed; didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The highest level of the defence was in Sarajevo, because that was the republican headquarters, or the centre of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's right. And indeed, the JNA shifted its allegiance to the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA came to Bosnia-Herzegovina, too, so I think that they really focused on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The point I'm making, I'm talking about after the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina was at that stage a foreign force in a sense, because it was a military force that had aligned itself to the Republic of Serbia; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so then, the defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was then left largely to the remnants of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And indeed, whatever JNA facilities came available to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might explain, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can explain the situation with a large military warehouse where Territorial Defence weapons were stored for the territory of some ten municipalities. It was in Sljmena near Travnik. And this warehouse was taken over by force, but the army had mined certain facilities, certain storage houses. So, these warehouses and military facilities were not in all cases made available to the Territorial Defence. Things were done by force, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right and I should have been more cautious with my generalisation. Certainly there was a number of instances where the JNA itself took over resources of the Territorial Defence, and I wasn't disputing that. I was talking more about facilities such as the Kaonik facility, it was a former JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was taken over by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But we don't need to dwell on that. I'm just trying to see if you can assist me with the general background. Now, apart from the Territorial Defence units which were organised during the course of 1992, from Sarajevo; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, you tell us what the position is, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The units of the Territorial Defence were organised on the basis of this law that I spoke of, and they were organised in that particular way. And later on there were no new ways of organising it. It was as they were when they were multi-ethnic. The units of the Territorial Defence were, I mean later, in the Territorial Defence units, I mean, they were only formally called TO, Territorial Defence, but these were really units of the Muslim Bosniaks. So, it was not really in line with the regulations originally envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They couldn't be in line with the regulations originally envisaged, could they, because the whole top of the legislative structure had been removed: Namely, the Socialist Federal Republic no longer existed; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But what remained was the level at the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that continued, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it didn't exactly continue to function. It was supposed to continue functioning, but because of the actual state of affairs that prevailed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it could not function. I mean, they couldn't operate as Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to tell me about the practical circumstances as such, I'm talking about the legislative structure. We can come back to that. It's true Sarajevo was under siege and communications with municipalities was complicated; but would you agree there was still a government in Sarajevo and it was still purported, whether or not it was accepted, it was still purported to be the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, but the regulations remained the same. No new regulations were passed by that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. And indeed, the regulations which you relied on at the municipal level were the same regulations that applied prior to the breakup of the Socialist Republic, which is consistent with what applied in Sarajevo at the republic level. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, when you said earlier in your evidence that your reporting responsibilities as such from the municipal level went from the municipality up to the regional or military district level, which was Bosnia-Herzegovina; that in effect didn't change, surely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, this military district no longer existed, now there was a Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the Ministry of Defence was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so, you would have had to report to the Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you report to the Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo during the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And a few times I met with the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the purposes of your meeting with the Minister of Defence in Sarajevo, or wherever you met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before 1992, before the attack on Sarajevo, I met him then. And the point was to see what we were supposed to do under such circumstances, when certain units were turning against the people, and those were the units for which we supplied conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think you misheard my question. I asked you during the course of 1993 did you report to the Minister of Defence or the Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't, because there was no communication. The communication was cut off before that, as early as 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that is also because the military forces that were operational in the area of the municipality for which you were responsible was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning I was responsible for all the military forces and the territory of the municipality until February or March, 1992. And later on, later on Muslims, Bosniaks who were in the secretariat, they would mobilise people for their units and we Croats would mobilise people for Croatian units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and in particular that was the position in 1993 when the HVO was in conflict with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time all links in terms of joint efforts were cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the law that applied to, at a municipal level and at a republican level continued on; did it not, in 1993? I'm talking about these laws that you've been referring to, the old laws of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken over. They did not remain in the same form. The organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina took over these regulations as the organs of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna took over these same regulations. In fact, we worked according to the same regulations, but we got them from different authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, they were taken over by, at least at the level of the republic, they were taken over by the government or by the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the old SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where in the law of the Socialist Federal Republic or at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is there a provision which deals with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In these regulations there is not a single provision regulating the work of the HVO. This is in the regulations of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna at that time. But the regulations are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How do you say that the regulations that relate to the recruiting of civilians could be applied by the HVO when there was no link between that -- and I'm talking about no legislative link -- between that and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The continuity of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was severed at that point, and we Croats that lived in that area through the institution of Herceg-Bosna, we ensured our existence within the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in order to facilitate communication, in order to facilitate supplies, but not for Croats only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, within that territorial area of Herceg-Bosna, you declared yourself independent, whether it be directly or by implication, from the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I worked in the municipality, I did not proclaim myself independent of anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You may have done, but you say that the laws were applied by the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna in relation to that territory as something separate and distinct from the laws that were applied by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Sarajevo; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that the regulations were different, I said they were the same; but the preamble, the organ who handed it down to us was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you're not able to show us or point to anything which permitted, as a matter of law, for the HVO to operate as an independent military unit on this territory; are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, on the basis of which we functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course. And no doubt the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna passed many laws during this period, and I'm not quarrelling with that. What I'm asking you, though, is to point to the law that permits that community to enact its own laws and to adopt regulations such as these.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that's because there is no law; is there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should just like to draw your attention to one point and to make an objection to the Prosecution. During the witness's statement, the witness did not use any legal acts which were brought in by the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. What he used was the legal act which was applied for the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina according to the principle of taking it over from federal regulations, the former federal regulations. As opposed to this, my learned colleague the Prosecutor implied that he referred to acts which were enacted within the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. That was not the case, and I should like to make an objection in that sense for the Prosecution's method of examination. And I should also like to make an objection in view of the fact that my learned colleague, with his questions, out stepped the boundaries of the questions asked by the defence. My colleague, the Prosecutor is asking the witness things about political organisational structures, which we did not bring up in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, firstly, there seems to be this myth that cross-examination is limited only to what is raised in evidence-in-chief and I think we have canvassed this on numerous occasions before. In no jurisdiction where cross-examination is a feature of the adversarial trial process am I aware of any situation where cross-examination is limited only to matters raised in-chief. Cross-examination is regulated by whether it is relevant or not, or harassing, or other rules; but never have I known it to be limited to simply matters raised in-chief. Secondly, dealing with the other issue, it's a little bit disingenuous for the Defence to call a witness before the Chamber who purports to lay before you the foundation upon which they say they and others acted in this particular region during 1993, and say this is the legal foundation of it then to object when I seek to explore the foundation of this law. It's all very well to pull a law out of the air and say it was relied on, and it's another matter, indeed, to say this is the legislative foundation of that law on which we relied. And it's the legislative foundation which I'm seeking to explore. Because, Your Honours, if we can be pointed to know legitimate legislative foundation, then it doesn't matter what the law is, it has no application. And I presume what is sought to be done at the end of the day is to be said, well, all these people did engage in trench digging but it was done in accordance with the law; so therefore, there is nothing wrong because people were taken out in accordance with the law. If that's what is sought to be achieved, and I assume that's what Mr. Mikulicic is seeking to do, then it's entirely appropriate for me to say, what is this law, and what is its foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I have discussed the matter with my colleagues and the Trial Chamber thinks that the Defence has called this witness in order for the witness to explain to the Trial Chamber the legal foundations of the laws governing the units of civilian work. At least that's how we have understood the calling by the Defence of this witness. But we also think that the goal of the Defence is to give to the Trial Chamber a certain number of informations relating to the political military problems, the problems arising from the arrival of refugees in the region, the problems of detention of certain civilians by the Croats, all this, of course, within the framework of the territory of the Lasva Valley. This is what interests us directly, as this is what is directly linked to the charges brought against Mr. Aleksovski. We are interested about what happened in Kaonik and in the Lasva Valley area. We always have to keep this in mind, we want some general information on the general background prevailing at the time, and I think Mr. Neimann is quite right, it is always useful to repeat time and again that what has happened in the Lasva Valley are the very heart of the case against Mr. Aleksovski. Yet, we cannot limit ourselves exclusively to the Kaonik camp. We have to try to understand the general background of this case. Therefore, the Trial Chamber, taking all this into account, decides that Mr. Neimann is entitled to put any questions he wishes to the witness, and the witness will just answer these questions if he is able to give an answer to these questions. This is our decision, and, Mr. Neimann, you are invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, Mr. Rajic, my question was that there was no foundation law which permitted the adoption of these old laws by the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna? That was my question. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You said that that is your opinion. I simply can't recall everything. A lot of time has gone by. But, I think that we did have regulations according to which we functioned in the municipalities and which were legal, so to speak, lawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell on this topic, Mr. Rajic, for much longer. I merely wanted to ask you, if you could, to point to any such law, but I understand entirely. It's been some time now if you're unable to do that. If you're unable to do that, please just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a regulation here with me. This is a regulation relating to the armed forces of Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna adopted on the 3rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that was adopted by the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But just to complete this point, you can't point to a law of either the federal former socialist federal Republic of Yugoslavia or a law of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which would permit the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna to adopt or apply these laws? And that's my point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't show you that now, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on, if I may, to these local work units that were established. Can you tell us where they were operational, geographically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were operational in every municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were they operational in the Municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They should have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any connection with supplying civilian work units to the Busovaca area or municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, who is responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I should have told you and I'm sorry I didn't. I am talking about 1993 in that period of time. I have moved forward to 1993. I am asking you, during the first half of 1993, were you in any way involved, yourself, personally, in relation to the supply of civilian work units to the Municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well can you tell me who was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the department for the defence of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you have any connection whatsoever with the department of the defence of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your connection to the department of defence of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, with the head we would exchange experiences with the head of the department of how, in the best possible way, we could work under the given circumstances which were very difficult indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you in a position of authority or superior to the head of the department of defence of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you couldn't give any orders or directions in relation to what happened in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you limited only to the Municipality of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So all of the evidence that you've given here today relates merely -- well, won't say merely, I withdraw that. Relates entirely to the Municipality of Travnik and no other municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the functioning and collecting the units of the work duties, this refers to all the municipalities. Because that was the method of work in all the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, who was responsible overall for the function and collecting of the units for work duties? Was that you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among others, I was one of them, but there were the commanders of the units if a situation required this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the commanders of the units would be commanders of the HVO units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the HVO, the commanders of the HVO, if it was their members. If it was the HV, then it would be those commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And isn't it true that you were responsible for the HVO units? And I say that, perhaps I should clarify that for you. Responsible for the HVO units in supplying, ultimately, the civilian work facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It wasn't very clear and I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what sense am I responsible?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Let me break up the question a bit for you. I am not asking you about what happened right down the command level. I accept what you say, that from time to time commanders could recruit civilians to carry out -- will carry out work duties for them. I accept that as part of the chain of command they could do that. But you're in a position, were you not, above the level of the commanders and you had a direct involvement with the civilian work duties that were carried out, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
